title: Round 6 — Both Sides of the Channel

questions.question: About 90% of the mustard seeds used to make traditional Dijon mustard are imported from which country?
questions.note: Local Burgundy farmers largely switched to subsidised rapeseed, so most seed for Dijon mustard now comes from the Canadian prairies.

questions.question: In what year did Henry VIII of England and François I of France meet in extravagant splendour near Calais, at the summit known as the Field of the Cloth of Gold?
questions.imageAlt: A crowded 16th-century painting of a royal summit with tents, a golden castle and processions
questions.imageCredit: The Field of the Cloth of Gold, c.1545, Royal Collection · Wikimedia Commons (public domain)
questions.note: The lavish 18-day meeting near Calais began on 7 June 1520, each king trying to out-dazzle the other.

questions.question: In which Paris museum is this painting — Leonardo da Vinci's Mona Lisa — displayed?
questions.imageAlt: A famous Renaissance portrait of a woman with an enigmatic smile
questions.imageCredit: Mona Lisa, Leonardo da Vinci · Wikimedia Commons (public domain)
questions.note: Leonardo brought the painting to France in 1516, and it has hung in the Louvre since the late 1790s.

questions.question: What is the highest mountain in England, rising to 978 metres in the Lake District?
questions.note: Scafell Pike in Cumbria is England's highest peak at 978 m (3,209 ft).

questions.question: The modern Olympic Games were revived by which Frenchman, who founded the International Olympic Committee at the Sorbonne in Paris in 1894?
questions.note: Coubertin convened delegates from nine nations at the Sorbonne on 23 June 1894 to create the IOC and revive the Games.

questions.question: English borrowed 'nonchalant' from French. What does it describe about a person's manner?
questions.note: 'Nonchalant' comes from Old French 'non' (not) plus a verb meaning 'to care' — literally someone who does not care.

questions.question: In the traditional method used to make Champagne, where does the second fermentation that creates the bubbles take place?
questions.note: The méthode champenoise triggers a second fermentation inside each sealed bottle, trapping the CO₂ that gives Champagne its fizz.

questions.question: Eleanor of Aquitaine was queen consort of which two neighbouring kingdoms, first by marriage to Louis VII and then to Henry II?
questions.note: She was Queen of France until her 1152 annulment, then Queen of England from 1154 — and mother of Richard the Lionheart.

questions.question: Which French composer wrote the 1928 orchestral work Boléro, famous for its single long crescendo?
questions.note: Boléro was commissioned as a ballet by the dancer Ida Rubinstein and premiered at the Paris Opéra in November 1928.

questions.question: What is the highest mountain in Wales, known in Welsh as Yr Wyddfa?
questions.note: Snowdon (Yr Wyddfa) reaches 1,085 m, the highest point in Britain south of the Scottish Highlands.

questions.question: In French, the English-derived word 'un lifting' refers to which cosmetic procedure?
questions.note: French took English 'lifting' to mean a facelift — one of many '-ing' words the language borrowed and repurposed.

questions.question: According to sporting legend, at which English school did William Webb Ellis first pick up the ball and run with it in 1823, giving his name to rugby?
questions.note: The tale is folklore rather than proven fact, but the Rugby World Cup trophy is still the Webb Ellis Cup in his honour.

questions.question: In what year did the English longbow win the Battle of Crécy against the French during the Hundred Years' War?
questions.note: Edward III's archers routed a much larger French army on 26 August 1346.

questions.question: What is the largest natural lake lying entirely within France, near Aix-les-Bains in Savoie?
questions.note: Lac du Bourget in Savoie is the largest natural lake wholly inside France, about 18 km long — and inspired a famous poem by Lamartine.

questions.question: Blue Stilton cheese has a Protected Designation of Origin restricting it to three English counties: Leicestershire, Nottinghamshire and which other?
questions.note: Only these three counties may make Stilton — which means the Cambridgeshire village of Stilton itself isn't allowed to produce it.

questions.question: In standard French the number 70 is 'soixante-dix'. What do those two words mean, added together, literally?
questions.note: French keeps a leftover of an old base-20 count, so 70 is spoken as 'sixty-ten' (Belgium and Switzerland instead say 'septante').

questions.question: Which British author created the Belgian detective Hercule Poirot?
questions.note: Poirot first appeared in Christie's 1920 debut novel, The Mysterious Affair at Styles.

questions.question: In a standard frame of snooker, what is the highest possible break a player can make without the opponent committing a foul?
questions.note: It comes from potting all 15 reds each with a black, then the six colours in sequence.

questions.question: Mary, Queen of Scots was raised in France and briefly became queen consort of France by marrying which king, the Dauphin she wed in 1558?
questions.note: Their 1558 marriage made her Queen of France when Francis became king in 1559 — though he died barely a year later.

questions.question: In the traditional Cornish way of preparing a cream-tea scone, which is spread on first: the jam or the clotted cream?
questions.note: The Cornish spread jam first, then top it with clotted cream — the reverse of the Devon method.

questions.question: Which strait separates the French island of Corsica from the Italian island of Sardinia?
questions.note: The Strait of Bonifacio is the roughly 11 km channel between Corsica to the north and Sardinia to the south.

questions.question: Which English animator created Wallace & Gromit at Bristol's Aardman studio?
questions.note: Park has won multiple Oscars for the clay-animated pair, beginning with A Grand Day Out in 1989.

questions.question: The original FIFA World Cup trophy, used from 1930 to 1970, was named after which Frenchman, the FIFA president who launched the tournament?
questions.note: Rimet, FIFA president from 1921 to 1954, drove the creation of the first World Cup, held in Uruguay in 1930.

questions.question: In the French 'galette des rois' eaten around Epiphany, what is the little charm hidden inside called?
questions.note: 'Fève' means broad bean — the original token, now usually a porcelain figurine; whoever finds it is crowned king or queen for the day.

questions.question: Which British monarch officially opened the Channel Tunnel in 1994, alongside French President François Mitterrand?
questions.note: The Queen and Mitterrand inaugurated the rail tunnel on 6 May 1994, meeting in the middle beneath the sea.

questions.question: In the Chaîne des Puys of the Massif Central, which lava-dome volcano gives its name to the surrounding French département?
questions.note: The Puy de Dôme (1,465 m) is the tallest volcano of the Chaîne des Puys, near Clermont-Ferrand.

questions.question: The classic British summer drink Pimm's No. 1 Cup is based on which spirit?
questions.note: Pimm's No. 1, first produced by James Pimm in 1823, is a gin-based fruit cup usually served with lemonade and chopped fruit.

questions.question: Which French Impressionist painted views of Upper Norwood and Sydenham while sheltering in south London during the Franco-Prussian War of 1870–71?
questions.imageAlt: An Impressionist painting of a snowy suburban lane with a few small figures
questions.imageCredit: Fox Hill, Upper Norwood (1870), Camille Pissarro · Wikimedia Commons (public domain)
questions.note: This is the very picture — about a dozen of his London-exile paintings survive, and Fox Hill, Upper Norwood now hangs in the National Gallery.

questions.question: Football's world governing body FIFA was founded in 1904 in which European capital city?
questions.note: FIFA was founded on 21 May 1904 in Paris, with the Frenchman Robert Guérin as its first president.

questions.question: In England, town names ending in '-by' (Whitby, Grimsby, Derby) come from the language of which settlers?
questions.note: '-by' is an Old Norse word for a farmstead or village, left across the Danelaw by Viking settlers.
